query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A combined high-throughput computational approach—integrating advanced CALPHAD modeling with atomistic simulations (using MD with advanced MEAM potentials and hybrid MC/MD annealing)—can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and volume change at melting, as well as liquid-phase thermodynamic properties, in equiatomic and near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with an expected error margin of less than a minor error compared to direct high-temperature experimental measurements. This method operates by capturing the essential multicomponent mixing effects that govern the melting and fusion transitions in HEAs.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase high-entropy alloys in the solid solution state (e.g., refractory HEAs like Nb–Mo–Ta–W–V, equiatomic Cantor-type alloys, and related compositions) prepared via conventional melting routes.
generation.intervention: Implement integrated simulations combining CALPHAD liquid and solid thermodynamic models with atomistic MD (and MC/MD for structure evolution) to predict the melting point, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and associated volume changes. Then validate these predictions using high-temperature differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in-situ neutron imaging during controlled heating and cooling experiments.
generation.conditions: Experiments and simulations performed over a wide temperature range—from room temperature up to above the solidus temperature—under well-controlled inert (or vacuum) atmospheres to avoid oxidation. Simulation conditions must include realistic potential parameterizations and configurational sampling (e.g., grain sizes spanning nano- to micro-scale) to capture both bulk and grain boundary effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering and grain-boundary characteristics mediate atomic diffusion and phase nucleation during melting and fusion; these are captured via short-range order (SRO) parameters and next-neighbor bond counting in the simulations.
generation.mechanism: The approach relies on the fact that the fusion properties in HEAs arise from a balance between configurational (mixing) entropy and thermal contributions. Advanced MD simulations with advanced MEAM potentials capture local atomic rearrangements and volume changes at melting, while CALPHAD models incorporate non-ideal mixing in both solid and liquid phases. The combined method accounts for gradual changes, such as the two-stage melting observed in polycrystalline systems, and predicts the thermodynamic forces driving phase transitions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Simulated melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies and entropies, and volume changes at melting are expected to agree within ±10% of the experimental DSC and neutron imaging data. Furthermore, the computed liquid-phase free energy and non-ideality should match observed two-stage melting phenomena (e.g., pre-melting at grain boundaries followed by bulk melting) in polycrystalline HEAs.
generation.baseline: Traditional high-temperature DSC measurements, calorimetry, and neutron imaging data reported for systems such as Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 and equiatomic CoCrFeMoNi, alongside established MD simulation studies predicting melting behavior in HEAs.
generation.boundary: This integrated approach is expected to be most accurate for HEAs with equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions that exhibit a single-phase or moderately segregated structure. It may be less applicable or require further refinement for alloys with strong eutectic reactions, extensive amorphization under rapid cooling, or where long-range ordering dominates the melting behavior.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty arises primarily from (i) potential parameterization limitations in the MD models, (ii) extrapolation errors in CALPHAD databases when applied to higher-order systems, and (iii) experimental measurement variability at very high temperatures. Overall, these sources may introduce an uncertainty of approximately ±10% in predicted thermodynamic quantities.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of high-entropy alloys spanning different compositions (including canonical systems such as Nb–Mo–Ta–W–V and Cantor-type alloys). For each alloy, perform controlled DSC experiments and in-situ neutron imaging to acquire high-temperature melting profiles, fusion enthalpy/entropy data, and volume change measurements. Concurrently, execute the integrated CALPHAD+MD simulation protocol for the same compositions under identical thermal conditions.
measurements: DSC curves with clear endothermic/exothermic peaks identifying melting and crystallization events.
Density/volume measurements across the melting transition via neutron imaging or dilatometry.
Calculated fusion enthalpy and entropy values from the simulations.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, across multiple HEA compositions, the experimentally measured melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, or volume change at melting consistently differ by more than 15% from the integrated computational predictions, then the proposed approach is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe determined the entropy of high entropy alloys by investigating single-crystalline nickel and five high entropy alloys: two fcc-alloys, two bcc-alloys and one hcp-alloy. Since the configurational entropy of these single-phase alloys differs from alloys using a base element, it is important to quantify the entropy. Using differential scanning calorimetry, cp-measurements are carried out from −170 °C to the materials’ solidus temperatures TS. From these experiments, we determined the thermal entropy and compared it to the configurational entropy for each of the studied alloys. We applied the rule of mixture to predict molar heat capacities of the alloys at room temperature, which were in good agreement with the Dulong-Petit law. The molar heat capacity of the studied alloys was about three times the universal gas constant, hence the thermal entropy was the major contribution to total entropy. The configurational entropy, due to the chemical composition and number of components, contributes less on the absolute scale. The experimentally determined coherent domain size from diffraction studies were found to be also around 10 nm and it is expected that this thermodynamic simulation model should sufficiently capture the enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs free energy changes. Here the ΔH is taken from the difference of potential energies of the relaxed configurations of the evolved structure and the initial random structure. The melting mechanism of single crystal and polycrystalline Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) were investigated by the molecular dynamics (MD) simulation using the second-nearest neighbor modified embedded-atom method (2NN MEAM) potential. For the single crystal RHEA, the density profile displays an abrupt drop from 11.25 to 11.00 g/cm3 at temperatures from 2910 to 2940 K, indicating all atoms begin significant local structural rearrangement. For polycrystalline RHEAs, a two-stage melting process is found. In the first melting stage, the melting of the grain boundary (GB) regions firstly occurs at the pre-melting temperature, which is relatively lower than the corresponding system-melting point. At the pre-melting temperature, most GB atoms have enough kinetic energies to leave their equilibrium positions, and then gradually induce the rearrangement of grain atoms close to GB. In the second melting stage at the melting point, most grain atoms have enough kinetic energies to rearrange, resulting in the chemical short-ranged order changes of all pairs.
